articles.title: Marseille Reaches 17 Landings as Orange Activates Medusa's First Mediterranean Leg
articles.subtitle: Medusa's 1,050km France–North Africa segment goes live, connecting directly into Orange's Paris-region DC fibre ring.
articles.body_md:
On June 8, 2026, **Orange** activated the ViaTunisia segment of the **Medusa Submarine Cable System** — a **1,050km Marseille-to-Bizerte link** that marks the first live leg of the **€342M** 10-country Mediterranean cable system. It is the first new high-capacity France–North Africa corridor since Red Sea disruption began routing Atlantic-Asia traffic via the Cape of Good Hope, and it arrives as Marseille consolidates its position as Europe's densest submarine cable hub.

## What Medusa Is

The full Medusa system spans **8,760km** across **10 Mediterranean countries** — Morocco, Portugal, Spain, France, Algeria, Tunisia, Italy, Greece, Cyprus, and Egypt — with **16 landing points**, **24 fibre pairs**, and **20 Tbps capacity per pair**. It is the only submarine cable system designed to land in every major Mediterranean coastal state simultaneously. Led by **AFR-IX Telecom** with co-funding from the EU and Orange, and built by **Alcatel Submarine Networks**, the system adds redundant capacity to a corridor under acute stress: 17 cables remain disrupted in the Red Sea with no repair timeline. The Marseille landing is structurally notable beyond headline capacity: Orange connects ViaTunisia directly into an existing **fibre ring linking its Paris-region data centres**, making new capacity immediately accessible to Orange's wholesale and enterprise customers without an additional transit hop to a separate carrier. **Marseille** now hosts **17 submarine cable landings** — the highest concentration at any European Mediterranean port.

## The Sovereignty Calculus

For investors tracking the cable sovereignty thread, this adds complexity to the France–Italy dynamic. **Italy's €700M TIM Sparkle nationalisation** (Edition 13) placed the Mediterranean's primary routing contracts and infrastructure under state control — the MEF/Retelit structure gives Rome a veto over cable routing and hyperscaler contracts on the Hormuz/Red Sea alternative corridor. Marseille's 17-landing density creates a rival concentration of cable infrastructure under French digital infrastructure rather than Italian state ownership, and Medusa's €342M cost reflects EU co-funding discipline that TIM Sparkle's bilateral acquisition did not require.

As Medusa expands to Egypt, Greece, Cyprus, and Spain across the rest of 2026, the system becomes an alternative Mediterranean backbone independent of both TIM Sparkle routes and the disrupted Red Sea corridor. The question for the next 6–18 months: whether **hyperscalers** sign dedicated capacity agreements through **Orange's Marseille DC fibre ring** on Medusa, and whether AFR-IX's pricing for the Marseille–Egypt route competes with TIM Sparkle's established hyperscaler contracts on the same geography.
articles.summary: Orange activated the first leg of the €342M Medusa submarine cable system on June 8, connecting Marseille to Bizerte with 1,050km of high-capacity fibre. Marseille now hosts 17 cable landings, cementing its position as Europe's densest Mediterranean digital hub.

articles.title: France Fields Its Strongest AI Gigafactory Bid as AION's Eight-Member Consortium Submits €10B
articles.subtitle: Ardian, Orange, EDF, Iliad, and Capgemini combine in a 200MW-to-1GW bid that answers EuroHPC's sovereignty test — but faces a structural funding paradox.
articles.body_md:
On June 5, 2026, eight French organisations — **Ardian, Artefact, Bull (Atos), Capgemini, EDF, Iliad, Orange**, and **Scaleway** — formally submitted a bid for one of five EU AI Gigafactory designations under EuroHPC's live call. The **AION consortium** proposes a **€10B** total investment, **200MW** initial phase by 2030, scaling to **1 GW** — compute equivalent to more than **288,000 NVIDIA H100 GPUs** — the most comprehensive industrial coalition the programme has received.

## Why AION Is the Strongest French Bid

EuroHPC's core requirement is sovereignty across the full AI value chain. AION delivers: private equity (Ardian), sovereign cloud infrastructure (Scaleway/Iliad), national telco (Orange), energy utility (**EDF**, with nuclear baseload supply), defence IT (Bull/Atos), and enterprise consulting (Capgemini). **EDF**'s nuclear power commitment and **RTE**'s grid connection materially de-risk the question that has stalled competing bids in energy-constrained markets. With the **EuroHPC June 23 deadline** now closed, three to five designations are expected in July 2026 from approximately **10 formal bids**, down from **~70 expressions of interest** — a collapse that reflects the programme's structural funding problem: only **€4.1B of the €20B** has confirmed EU funding, with **€15.9B** in member-state and private co-investment unconfirmed.

## The Structural Paradox

AION's bid sits inside a paradox the entire EU AI Gigafactory programme faces. France already holds **SoftBank's €75B bilateral commitment** for 5 GW in Hauts-de-France (Edition 15) and the **Ardian/Verne €5B private campus** in Île-de-France (this edition) — both confirmed before a single EU designation has been made. The bilateral and private-capital tracks together represent more capital certainty than the EU programme's entire pre-2028 confirmed funding, which raises the question of what EU designation actually delivers. The answer is not capital but mandate: European Commission **open-access designation**, public computing allocation for academic and SME workloads, and sovereign branding that bilateral commercial deals cannot provide. AION's breadth — spanning every segment from power to workload — is optimised for precisely that mandate, not for commercial returns.

Competing bids include a **Telefónica-led** Spanish consortium, a **Deutsche Telekom** German bid, and Germany's **Schwarz Group** (Lidl/Kaufland parent), which has already commenced a **200+ MW** data centre south of Berlin without waiting for EU subsidy. EuroHPC selection results in July 2026 will test whether the programme's remaining credibility survives comparison with bilateral capital already moving at speed.
articles.summary: The AION consortium — Ardian, Orange, EDF, Iliad, Capgemini, and three others — submitted a €10B bid for EU AI Gigafactory designation on June 5, targeting 200MW by 2030 and 1GW total. The EuroHPC deadline closed June 23; three to five designations are expected in July 2026.

articles.title: Ardian and Verne Commit €5B to 500MW Paris-Region AI Campus — Three Simultaneous France DC Tracks Now Active
articles.subtitle: Private capital enters France independently of SoftBank and the EU gigafactory, targeting Paris-region latency with vertically integrated infrastructure, power, and workload access.
articles.body_md:
At the Choose France summit on **June 1, 2026**, **Ardian** and **Verne** announced a **€5B** AI and computing campus in **Île-de-France** — **500MW** total capacity, **200MW** first phase by 2030. The announcement reveals France's AI infrastructure investment wave operating on three simultaneous, structurally independent tracks — and the private capital track as the most vertically integrated.

## Three Tracks, One Market

**SoftBank's €75B** (Edition 15) targets 5 GW across greenfield Hauts-de-France industrial sites through 2031: bilateral government-endorsed, industrial-scale, **EDF** grid connection pending. The **AION consortium** (this edition) pursues EU gigafactory designation, securing Commission open-access mandate and the **€4.1B** confirmed EU pre-2028 tranche. Ardian/Verne operates on a third track entirely: no EU subsidy, no government guarantee, no publicly named hyperscaler anchor. The selection of **Île-de-France** — Paris-region proximity — over SoftBank's northern industrial sites signals deliberate market positioning: low-latency access for financial services and enterprise AI, not greenfield power capacity.

## Vertical Integration as Thesis

Ardian's structure is the most distinctive element of this thesis. The firm simultaneously manages the campus equity (**Verne** JV), energy supply (**Akuo** and **GreenYellow** renewables subsidiaries, **€3B committed**, **2.5 GW** by 2030), and workload access via the AION consortium computing mandate. This three-layer vertical — infrastructure, power, workload origination — is the most integrated private-capital AI DC thesis visible in Western Europe today. The implicit logic: owning both the electrons and the compute removes two of the three primary risk variables (power cost and PPA availability) from an investment that otherwise depends on market conditions for grid access.

At **€5B** for **500MW**, Ardian/Verne enters the same capital tier as **HSCALE Milan** (Edition 13, **€2B+**, 250MW) but at 2× the scale and targets primary-market Paris latency. **Equinix** and **Digital Realty** — whose FLAP-D strongholds have historically defined European hyperscale entry — face a private-capital competitor with operational credentials (Verne's Nordic DC heritage) and energy supply certainty that neither incumbent has matched in France. For infrastructure investors, France has moved from single-narrative (SoftBank bilateral) to multi-capital-structure competition in under six months. The next milestones — a hyperscaler pre-lease announcement for the Île-de-France campus, and confirmation that **Akuo/GreenYellow** renewable capacity can deliver coincident with the 2030 DC Phase 1 target — will determine whether the vertical integration thesis produces the returns that justify premium Paris-region capital costs.
articles.summary: Ardian and Verne announced a €5B, 500MW AI campus in Île-de-France at the Choose France summit on June 1, targeting 200MW by 2030 with no EU subsidy or named hyperscaler anchor. Ardian's simultaneous €3B French renewable energy programme creates a vertically integrated infrastructure, power, and workload thesis.

articles.title: UK Designates Five AI Growth Zones with Nscale £2.5B and Vantage £12B as First Anchors
articles.subtitle: Growth Zone status addresses the planning bottleneck but leaves the 24.67p/kWh electricity cost and 125GW Ofgem grid queue structurally unchanged.
articles.body_md:
On June 8, 2026, the UK government formally designated five **AI Growth Zones** with accelerated planning consent and priority grid access, and simultaneously confirmed **£2.5B** from **Nscale** and **£12B** from **Vantage** as the first private investment anchors. The package is the most substantive policy instrument for AI infrastructure the UK has deployed since January's AI Opportunities Action Plan — but it leaves the primary investment constraint, **industrial electricity at 24.67p/kWh** (~4× Nordic rates), structurally unchanged.

## The Five Zones and Their Anchors

The designated zones are **Culham** (Oxfordshire), **North East England**, **North Wales**, **South Wales**, and **Lanarkshire** (Scotland), with Lanarkshire backed by **£8.2B** in committed private investment and **3,400 projected high-skilled jobs**. **Nscale** commits its first UK data centre in **Loughton, Essex** — **45,000 NVIDIA GB200 GPUs**, targeted **Q4 2026** go-live — the same operator anchoring Norway's Narvik AI campus (**230MW, $4.2B**, Microsoft Rubin GPUs, Edition 13). **Vantage**'s **£12B** on the former **Ford Bridgend plant** in South Wales — a **10-building campus**, **11,500+ jobs** — is the largest single-site UK DC announcement by capital.

## What Growth Zone Status Solves and What It Doesn't

The Nscale dual footprint is the critical strategic signal. Narvik provides AI training compute at **~€0.04/kWh** with Norwegian state (Eksfin) backing; Essex provides UK-market-facing deployment for financial services and latency-sensitive enterprise. Operators with capital are bifurcating: energy-intensive training workloads go to energy-cheap geographies; compliance-driven and latency-sensitive workloads remain in the UK. Growth Zone designation accelerates planning — the **NSIP opt-in track** (Edition 12) already provides 12–24 month national approvals — but planning consent does not substitute for a binding grid connection.

The structural constraint remains the **Ofgem grid queue**: **125 GW** outstanding, approximately **50 GW** linked to data centres, with only **71 DCs (~20 GW)** at financial investment decision. Ofgem's Phase 1 connection reform — financial gatekeeping via refundable deposits, FID evidence, and planning permission as queue entry conditions — has been proposed but not yet enacted. The **tCSNP2** transmission plan refresh (due June 2026) will determine which grid corridors reach AI Growth Zone sites by 2028–2032. Until that plan is published and Ofgem's reform takes effect, Growth Zone designation addresses one bottleneck (planning) while leaving the binding constraint (power delivery cost and queue) unchanged. Nscale Loughton's Q4 2026 commissioning date is the first real-world test of whether a Growth Zone-backed project can secure a binding grid connection on that timeline.
articles.summary: The UK designated five AI Growth Zones on June 8 with Nscale committing £2.5B and Vantage committing £12B as anchor investors. Growth Zone status addresses planning timelines but does not resolve the 24.67p/kWh industrial electricity cost or the 125GW Ofgem grid queue.

articles.title: Germany's PUE ≤1.2 Mandate Triggers July 1 — EU-Wide Data Centre Labelling Finalised
articles.subtitle: The first hard efficiency threshold for European data centres arrives in nine days, making liquid cooling a regulatory requirement and establishing a cost floor the rest of Europe is watching.
articles.body_md:
On **July 1, 2026** — nine days away — any new data centre commissioned in Germany must achieve **PUE ≤1.2** under the country's Energy Efficiency Act, making Germany the first EU member state to legislate a hard performance threshold for data centre facilities. The European Commission has simultaneously finalised the **EED delegated regulation** establishing an EU-wide rating and labelling scheme across **24 Key Performance Indicators** — creating a two-level compliance architecture that will affect operators across every EU market.

## What the July 1 Threshold Requires

A PUE of **1.2** is substantially more demanding than the typical European new-build benchmark of **1.4–1.6**. Achieving it requires **liquid cooling infrastructure** designed from the ground up — not retrofitted — adding an estimated **€5–15M** on a **50MW** facility relative to an air-cooled baseline. That premium is manageable within European greenfield capex envelopes (**€400–800M** for a hyperscale campus), but it establishes a German-specific cost floor and a design requirement that changes the pipeline: operators with German projects in planning must commit to liquid cooling now or lose commercial viability post-July 1.

A second threshold follows from **January 2027**: **100% renewable electricity** mandatory for all German data centres. Together, the two requirements make Germany the most energy-regulation-intensive EU data centre market, with implications for operators already holding long-term green power contracts — a compliance advantage for those who have pre-signed German renewables PPAs.

## The EU-Wide Layer

The EC's finalised EED delegated regulation adds a **public transparency layer** on top of Germany's national thresholds. Operators with EU facilities above **500kW IT load** have been required to report annually to the **European Database on Data Centres** since June 2024. The new June 2026 labelling regulation adds **public performance scores** across PUE, **WUE** (water use), **ERF** (energy reuse), and **REF** (renewables fraction). Poor scores on non-energy KPIs will create investor and enterprise-customer scrutiny independent of compliance status — a reputational mechanism layered on top of the regulatory one.

**France, the Netherlands, Ireland**, and **Belgium** are monitoring Germany as a reference point before legislating equivalent hard thresholds. None have yet done so. For liquid cooling suppliers — **Vertiv**, **Schneider Electric**, and **Rittal** — July 1 creates structurally different German pipeline demand. Watch the first German new-build post-July 1 for confirmation of liquid cooling adoption; EU labelling public database launch date; and whether France or the Netherlands accelerate national efficiency thresholds in response.
articles.summary: Germany's PUE ≤1.2 mandate for new data centres takes effect July 1, 2026, making liquid cooling design a regulatory requirement and setting a cost floor of €5–15M per 50MW facility. The EC simultaneously finalised an EU-wide labelling scheme across 24 KPIs, adding public performance scoring to all facilities above 500kW IT load across EU member states.

articles.title: EU Merger Guidelines Consultation Closes Today — SFR Review Framework Now in Play
articles.subtitle: The first rewrite of EU horizontal merger guidelines in 22 years codifies 'loss of investment competition' as a standalone theory of harm, reshaping the Phase 2 risk calculus for the €20.35B SFR acquisition.
articles.body_md:
On **June 26** — today — the public consultation closes on the European Commission's **Draft Revised Horizontal Merger Guidelines**, ending the comment phase on the competition policy framework that will govern the review of the **€20.35B SFR three-way acquisition** and every major European telecom consolidation that follows. The draft is the first revision to the **2004 guidelines** in 22 years, and its core innovation — codifying **"loss of investment competition"** as a standalone theory of harm — is structurally targeted at the type of deal SFR represents.

## What the Draft Framework Changes

The 2004 guidelines allowed consolidating parties to invoke a **2-year investment benefit horizon**: demonstrate that scale enables network investment the acquirer couldn't achieve standalone, and regulators apply a proportionality test. The draft abandons this mechanism and introduces a new test: did the absorbed operator act as an independent competitive **investment driver** whose elimination reduces market-wide investment pressure? For SFR specifically, the answer is direct — **Bouygues** has been France's most aggressive mobile network investor over the past five years. Its integration into a consolidated entity removes Bouygues as an independent investment-competing operator, which is precisely the harm the draft articulates.

**GSMA** and **ETNO** submitted industry responses this week arguing the framework does not go far enough in recognising the investment rationale for consolidation. They are calling for an **investment productivity test** that measures scale benefits against competitive harm at a system level. If the Commission accepts these modifications in the final text, the framework tilts back toward permissiveness and the SFR defence case improves. Final guidelines adoption is expected **Q4 2026**.

## The Race Between Framework and Filing

The SFR timeline creates a structural race: filing before guidelines adoption triggers review under the more permissive 2004 framework; filing after adoption — expected H2 2026 for formal SFR pre-notification — triggers the new investment competition harm test. **SFR break-up fees** (€100M–€2B range, Edition 15) create real exit cost that constrains parties' ability to wait out regulatory uncertainty. The **Autorité de la Concurrence** president **Benoît Coeuré** has already telegraphed the AdC's posture (Edition 16: "ne va pas de soi"), citing the **2005 French price-collusion precedent**.

Parallel filing tracks add further complexity: **Bouygues/Orange** file with the AdC, while **Free/Iliad** must file with the European Commission due to non-French revenue weight — two simultaneous review tracks with potentially different analytical frameworks running as the final merger guidelines are adopted in parallel. The SFR transaction is the most regulatory-complex telecom deal in Europe since VodafoneThree. Watch final guidelines publication in Q4 2026 for whether the investment competition theory of harm is softened; SFR formal pre-notification timing; and the EC's treatment of the Romanian 4→3 precedent (minimal remedies) vs the SFR transaction scale.
articles.summary: The EU's first merger guideline rewrite in 22 years closes consultation on June 26, codifying 'loss of investment competition' as a standalone theory of harm for 4→3 telecom consolidations. GSMA and ETNO submitted responses calling for an investment productivity test; final guidelines adoption is expected Q4 2026, running concurrently with SFR's pre-notification window.
